newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Sparks cuts Argentine, Brazil 96/7 soybean outlook.
newsitem.headline: Sparks cuts Argentine, Brazil 96/7 soybean outlook.

text.p: Sparks said Monday bad weather made it cut its estimates for 1996/97 Argentine and Brazilian soybean crops to 11.9-12 million tonnes maximum from 13.7-14 million for Argentina, and to 26.4 million from 27 million for Brazil.

Sparks' South America Vice-president Juan Martin Rebolini told a conference Argentine 1996/97 soybean output could fall to 11.5 million tonnes if there is more bad weather. He also said the United States might have to import "a significant quantity" of soybeans if current trends continue."

"It's possible the United States will have to import a significant quantity of soybeans if sales continue like last week when China bought 150,000 tonnes of U.S. soybeans," said Rebolini, of the local office of U.S. agricultural consultancy Sparks Companies of Memphis, Tenn.

The combination of factors will mean a tight market for the moment, he said: "Only next year, if the U.S., Argentina and Brazilian crops come along well, could the ratio between stock and consumption begin to recover."
But he said high prices should help Argentine output hit 17 million tonnes and Brazilian output 31 million tonnes by 2005.
Rebolini said soybean prices could have further to rise.

"The international market is still not convinced (of damage to the Brazilian and Argentine crops), because the crop estimates of the United States Department of Agriculture and the Argentine Agricultural Secretariat still have not registered the real damage to the soy crops in Rio Grande do Sul and in Argentina," he said, "So it is foreseeable that the next few reports on supply and demand will be bullish."
Sparks Companies believes that the world has entered a new era of high soybean prices, which should rise to about $350 a tonne by 2005, Rebolini said.
